newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin meets leaders of Russia's neighbours.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin meets leaders of Russia's neighbours.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Saturday met the leaders of Ukraine, Georgia, Azebaijan and Armenia, hoping to improve strained relations with the ex-Soviet republics and rebuild Moscow's role in the post-Soviet world.
Yeltsin promised Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma he would visit Kiev in early June at the latest to end speculation about a growing rift between the two Slav neighbours.

He also held separate meeting with Azerbaijani President Haidar Aliyev and Armenian President Levon Ter-Petrosyan for talks on the prospects for settling the dispute between two Transcaucasus states over the Nagorno-Karabakh enclave.
Yeltsin later met Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze to discuss Moscow's role in settling the conflict between Tbilisi and its breakaway Black Sea region of Abkhazia.
The leaders of the ex-Soviet states took part in the summit meeting of the Commonwealth of Independendent States on Friday. Yeltsin on Saturday also met Kyrgyz President Askar Akayev.

Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as telling Kuchma he would visit Ukraine irrespective of whether the political treaty which the two states have been negotiating for some five years is ready or not.

Moscow and Kiev are at loggerheads over dividing up the former Soviet Black Sea fleet, in particular on where the Russian share of its warships should be based. Moscow and Kiev are also in disagreement on some economic and trade issues.

Some Russian political analysts have suggested that the unresolved problems between Moscow and Kiev and mutual suspicion between them could prompt Ukraine, which has so far stuck to political neutrality, to seek closer links with NATO.
"It's time to put an end (to Russian-Ukrainian disputes) because the whole world is speculating about our relations," Yeltsin told Kuchma.

Itar-Tass news agency said Yeltsin offered to focus on the protracted conflict over Karabakh, Azerbaijan's Armenian- populated region which broken away in the late 1980s, when he met the Armenian president.
Tens of thousands people were killed on both sides in fighting for Karabakh which ended in a truce in 1994.

Both Azerbaijan and Armenia, which backs the Karabakh separatists, have expressed dissatisfaction with Moscow's efforts to help them negotiate a lasting peace and have made clear they might consider other foreign mediators.

It was not clear whether at his meeting with Azerbaijan's Aliyev Yeltsin went beyond the Karabakh question and touched on the sensitive issue of the use of Russian pipelines to deliver oil from Baku's Caspian Sea deposits to Black Sea ports.

Azerbaijan has expressed doubts that Russia can effectively control the pipeline that runs though Chechnya, which is outside Moscow's control after the failure of Moscow's military campaign to subdue the breakaway north Caucasus region.
Russian political analysts have said that if Azerbaijan chooses to route its oil bypassing Russia, Moscow will lose much of its influence in the Transcaucasus regeion.
Yeltsin's press office said Yeltsin and the Georgian leader, Shevardnadze, discussed Russia's further peacekeeping role in breakaway Abkhazia.

Georgian nationalists have accused Moscow of pro-Abkhazian bias and have launched a campaign to replace Russian paratroopers, who man the dividing line between Georgian troops and separatist fighters, with peacekeepers from other countries.

During the Commonwealth summit Russia agreed to make its operations in Abkhazia more active and take under its control a wider buffer zone between troops and rebels. The Russian peacekeeping mandate has been extended to July.
